Does it help an agent to be told what kind of law it is looking for? The
question sounds easy and is easy to answer badly. Give one run the form of the
law and another nothing, and let the first also have more probes, a different
model, or easier settings to be judged on, and the comparison measures all of
those at once. A fair comparison changes **one** thing.

This lesson asks the question of a spring. A mass on a spring of hidden
stiffness is released at rest, and the agent can only read where the mass is
at a time of its choosing. The force law, $F = -kx$, is never seen directly; it
shows in the motion it causes. The same model probes the same spring three
times under the Discovery evaluation protocol: told the form of the motion
(**full**), told only the name of the parameter to report (**partial**), or
told nothing beyond the controls and the reading (**none**). Everything else is
held equal, and the build checks that it is.

The build then scores the three claims on the same held-out settings, sets
them beside baselines that use no model, and asks a second question the
scores alone cannot answer: did the readings each run collected contain the
answer, whatever the agent concluded from them?

## Assumptions

1. **The spring is simulated and linear.** The mass of one kilogram moves
   under $F = -kx$ with no friction (`pbc.mechanics.oscillator`), so a release
   at rest from amplitude $A$ gives $x(t) = A\cos\omega t$ with
   $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$. A claim is an angular frequency $\omega$; the
   stiffness follows as $k = m\omega^2$. A spring with friction or a stiffening
   force would be outside the family, and no claim could be right.
2. **The readings are noisy, the noise is known and repeatable.** Each reading
   has Gaussian noise; the same setting gives the same reading, so the replay
   is exact.
3. **Only the task text differs between conditions.** The model, the system
   prompt, the tools and their bounds, the budget of probes, the step limit,
   the seed, the tolerance, and the held-out settings are those of one
   protocol object. The owner of the project set this as a condition of the
   lesson, and a cell below checks it.
4. **The tools are part of every condition.** The tool that takes the claim
   names its parameter "omega, angular frequency" in all three conditions,
   because the claims must be comparable. Even under **none** the agent learns
   that an angular frequency is wanted, which is a hint at an oscillation.
5. **One run per condition.** Each condition was run once, on one seed. That is
   enough to show the protocol and to read three runs carefully; it is not
   enough to say which condition is better.

## A force law seen through its motion {#explanation}

For a mass $m$ on a spring of stiffness $k$, Newton's second law and Hooke's
law give

$$
m\ddot x = -kx, \qquad x(0) = A,\ \dot x(0) = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x(t) = A\cos(\omega t),\quad \omega = \sqrt{k/m}.
$$

The motion does not depend on the amplitude except through the factor $A$:
the period is the same for a small swing and a large one. That is the signature
of a linear force, and an agent can test it by releasing from two amplitudes
and comparing $x/A$ at the same time.

**Where to probe.** A reading at time $t$ constrains the phase $\omega t$. An
error $\delta\omega$ in the frequency shifts the phase by $t\,\delta\omega$,
which grows with time. So a reading at a late time constrains $\omega$ more
than an early one with the same noise, as long as the time is known: from
$x/A = \cos(\omega t)$ one gets $\omega t$ only up to the branches of the
arccosine, and the early readings tell which branch a late one is on. A large
amplitude makes the relative noise small. The probes allowed run up to a few
seconds; the claim is scored at later times, where a small error in $\omega$
has grown into a large error in the position.

**The score.** As in the force-law lesson, the held-out error is the
root-mean-square difference between the claim's prediction and the noise-free
motion at the held-out settings, here relative to the amplitude (the
displacement passes through zero). The law is recovered when the error is at
most `{python} result["tolerance"]` and the run ended on its own.

times and `submit` once to state its claim, in at most `{python} result["max-steps"]`
messages of at most `{python} result["max-calls"]` tool calls each. Calls
beyond that number in one message are refused unrun and cost no probe. It may
not run code, read a file, reach the network, or call the judge.

## Worked examples

### The three recorded runs

All three were recorded on the same day by the same Claude model working in a
Claude Code session, each as a fresh sub-agent that was given the system
prompt, its task, and the tool descriptions, and nothing else. It chose every
call after reading the readings the harness computed. None of them knew of
the other two.

evidence="d2-scores replay-full replay-partial replay-none"} The three claims

times are late, and a small error in $\omega$ has grown into a phase error
there.

### What the readings supported

Each run spent `{python} result["probes"]` probes. Fit the motion to the
readings of each run, exactly those its agent saw:

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.probe_fits)
```

```{python}
#| label: d2-probe-fits
#| echo: false
result.table("d2-probe-fits")
```

[The readings of every one of the three runs determine the frequency well
enough to recover the law: a least-squares fit to each run's own readings has a
held-out error within the tolerance.]{.claim type="numerically-verified"
scope="the readings of the three recorded runs" evidence="d2-probe-fits"} The
difference between the conditions is therefore not in the information the
agents collected. It is in what each agent concluded from it. The **full**
agent read the frequency off its late readings and said why. The **partial**
agent averaged estimates from early and late times with equal weight, and the
early ones, whose phase is least sensitive to the frequency, pulled the mean
away. The last column says how far each claim is from what its data support,
in units of the fit's standard error.

The figure shows errors of simulated runs that this build scored again. The
gap between a dark bar and the light bar beside it is the cost of the agent's
own reasoning, measured against what its readings supported. Its size is not a
property of the condition: with one run each, it could be the luck of one
estimate.

### Run the agents yourself

This needs your own key and costs a few cents per run. The build does not run
it, so the commands are marked.

::: {.not-verified}
```bash
uv sync --locked --no-dev --extra openai
export OPENAI_API_KEY="..."
cd site/lessons/agents-llm/06-prior-knowledge-in-discovery
uv run --locked --no-dev --extra openai python -m pbc.discovery.force_lab prior-full prior-partial prior-none
```
:::

With `--record` the command writes the fixture of each condition in the
current directory. A comparison worth stating needs many runs per condition,
on several seeds; such a benchmark runs outside the build and would be marked
"not verified" here.

## Limits {#limits}

- **One run per condition cannot rank the conditions.** The full condition
  recovered and the others did not, but a second run of each could reverse
  that. The page shows a protocol and three runs, not an effect of prior
  knowledge.
- **The conditions leak through the tools.** The claim's parameter is named
  and described in every condition. Under **none** the agent still learns that
  an angular frequency is wanted.
- **The family is fixed.** A claim is one frequency of an undamped linear
  spring. An agent that suspected friction or a non-linear force could not say
  so in its claim, only in its words, which are not scored.
- **The agents computed without code.** They estimated the frequency in their
  heads from the readings; the harness gives no calculator. A fit is what a
  calculator would have given, and the gap is partly arithmetic.
- **Simulated, not measured.** Nothing here is a reading of a real spring.
- **The recordings are not API runs.** They are Claude Code sessions, told by
  the session to answer in the harness's format and to use no tool of their
  own. A run through the provider API may differ, and the sessions reported
  no token count or price.

::: {.exercise .self-check}
The full condition recovered the law and the other two did not, on the same
held-out settings. What does this comparison support?

::: {.choices}
::: {.choice}
That telling an agent the form of the law makes it recover the law.

::: {.feedback}
There is one run per condition. A single success and two failures are
consistent with no effect at all, and the fits show that every run had the
information it needed.
:::
:::

::: {.choice correct="true"}
That on these three runs the agents' conclusions, not the readings they
collected, decided the outcome, and that more runs are needed to say anything
about the conditions.

::: {.feedback}
Right. The fits to each run's own readings all recover the law; the claims
differ because of how each agent estimated the frequency.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
That the none condition is better than the partial one, because its error is
smaller.

::: {.feedback}
Both failed, and with one run each the order of two failures says nothing.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.solution}
It supports a statement about three runs: under one protocol, with everything
but the task equal, the full run's claim predicts the held-out settings within
the tolerance and the other two do not, while the readings of all three runs
would have supported a recovery. The difference lies in each agent's estimate,
not in its data. It does not support a statement about the conditions: that
needs many runs per condition and seed, and a test of whether the difference in
recovery rates is larger than chance.
:::
:::

## Exercises

::: {.exercise}
The agents spent `{python} result["probes"]` probes each; the baselines spent `{python} result["budget"]`. Give the grid and
random baselines the same 8 probes on the same spring, and say whether they
still recover the law.

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.the_agents_budget)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("small-budget")
```

With the agents' number of probes the grid fails and the random settings
recover the law here. The grid's fit is consistent with the noise and still
wrong: with so few distinct times, another frequency, an alias whose cosine
passes through the same few readings, fits them as well as the right one. The
chi-square cannot tell the two apart; the held-out settings can. A few
well-chosen probes, as the agents' fits show, do better than a few regular ones
placed without regard to the phase.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
An error $\delta\omega$ in the frequency shifts the phase at time $t$ by
$t\,\delta\omega$. For the claim of the partial condition, take the difference
from the fit of its own readings as $\delta\omega$, and compute the phase shift
at 3 s, the latest time the tools accept, and at 9 s. Why does a claim that
looks close at the probed times fail later?

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.phase_shift)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("phase-shift")
```

The phase shift grows in proportion to the time. At the latest probed time it
is small, so the claim's prediction differs from the readings by about the
noise, and the agent could not see its error there. At three times that time the same
error is three times larger in phase, and the predicted position, which is the
amplitude times the cosine of the phase, is off by a fraction of the amplitude
that exceeds the tolerance. Scoring at settings beyond the probed range is what
exposes it.
:::
:::
